questions.q: Why isn't a deployed smart contract a complete product on its own?
options: It just holds state and exposes functions — it can't fetch data, push updates, or act on a schedule by itself
Smart contracts cannot store any data on the blockchain
Contracts are automatically deleted after a fixed number of transactions
A contract requires a paid license to accept function calls
questions.explain: A contract passively exposes functions and holds state; nothing about it runs proactively, fetches off-chain data, or reacts to events on its own.

questions.q: Why can't a browser wallet alone replace a dApp's backend?
options: It can sign and call the chain directly, but can't run on a schedule, index history, or hold a server-side API key
Wallets are only able to read ETH balances, nothing else
Wallets cannot connect to any blockchain network
Browser wallets are blocked from calling smart contract functions
questions.explain: A wallet is a user-side signing tool; it has no persistent server process, so it can't do always-on jobs like listening for events or managing sessions.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six off-chain backend jobs this course covers?
options: Compiling Solidity contracts to EVM bytecode
Reading chain state such as a wallet's balance
Listening for on-chain events in real time
Managing user sessions and verifying signatures
questions.explain: Compiling Solidity is part of the on-chain/contract-development workflow, not the off-chain backend jobs (reads, writes, event listening, indexing, oracles, sessions) this course builds.

questions.q: What does "off-chain" mean in the context of this course?
options: Code that runs on a server you control, outside the EVM, that talks to the chain on the user's behalf
Any blockchain activity that happens on a testnet instead of mainnet
Data that is permanently unverifiable and untrustworthy
A transaction that has not yet been mined into a block
questions.explain: Off-chain means your own backend code, running outside the EVM, that reads from and writes to the chain over RPC — not a claim about trust or network.

questions.q: Which chapter sequence matches this course's roadmap?
options: Talking to the chain, then listening for events, then indexing, then oracles, then wallets & sessions
Deploying contracts, then auditing them, then launching a token sale
Writing Solidity, then testing with Hardhat, then publishing documentation
Building a frontend UI, then connecting a wallet, then styling with CSS
questions.explain: The course builds the off-chain backend job list in order, chapter by chapter: reads/writes, event listening, indexing, oracles, then wallets and sessions.
